system:
You are helping an airline pilot work out when to sleep during their next roster period.

You know what pilots know about fatigue: sleep before an early start is hard to get, the
body clock does not move as fast as an aircraft does, and the hours around 02:00 to 06:00
body time are when alertness is worst. Use that.

You are advisory. You do not rule on whether any duty is legal — the operator owns that.

Read it, then plan my sleep for the whole period.

About me:
- Home base: MAD
- Door-to-report commute at MAD: 85 minutes each way
- Commute at any other station (hotel to airport): 40 minutes each way
- The roster covers 2026-10-11 to 2026-11-09

Return your answer as a single fenced JSON block, and nothing after it.

```json
{
  "duties": [
    {
      "date": "YYYY-MM-DD",
      "kind": "flight" | "positioning" | "standby" | "training" | "off",
      "station": "IATA code where the duty starts",
      "endStation": "IATA code where the duty ends",
      "reportUtc": "ISO-8601 instant in UTC, or null for a day off",
      "endUtc": "ISO-8601 instant in UTC, or null for a day off",
      "sectors": [
        {
          "flightNo": "string",
          "origin": "IATA",
          "dest": "IATA",
          "depUtc": "ISO-8601 instant in UTC",
          "arrUtc": "ISO-8601 instant in UTC"
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "blocks": [
    {
      "kind": "main" | "pre-duty-nap" | "recovery-nap",
      "startUtc": "ISO-8601 instant in UTC",
      "endUtc": "ISO-8601 instant in UTC",
      "station": "IATA code where they will be sleeping",
      "why": "one sentence, in the words a crew member would use"
    }
  ],
  "conflicts": [
    {
      "ruleId": "the id of the rule this collides with",
      "date": "YYYY-MM-DD the collision lands on",
      "statement": "what collides, in plain language",
      "options": ["what they could do about it"]
    }
  ]
}
```

Rules for the JSON, all of which matter:

- **Every time is an absolute UTC instant.** The roster prints local time, or UTC, or
  both — say which it is using and convert. A time that is out by a timezone puts
  someone to bed at the wrong hour.
- **One entry per duty**, in date order, covering every date in the period including
  days off.
- `reportUtc` is when they are due at work. For a flight duty that is before the first
  sector's departure by the operator's reporting offset; for standby or training it is
  the stated start of the window, with no offset.
- **Always produce a plan.** If something in the roster is genuinely unreadable, still
  return your best reading and say so in a conflict — never return nothing.

content.text: I'll start by reading the roster.

I've read the roster. Key reading notes before the plan:

- **Times printed are LOCAL to the station shown** (report/STD at origin, STA/off-duty at destination). I've converted everything to UTC and cross-checked every sector against the printed block time — all 20 sectors reconcile, which confirms the timezone assumptions.
- **DST:** Europe goes back at 01:00 UTC on **25/10/2026**, so MAD/FCO are UTC+2 up to 24/10 and UTC+1 after; LHR is UTC+0 on 09/11. DXB +4, GRU −3, SIN +8, BOG −5 (no DST at any of those).
- **Reporting offset:** the roster prints report times directly — 1h30 before STD on long-haul, 1h00 on the FCO/LHR turnarounds. I've used the printed values. SIM and SBY start at the stated time with no offset.
- Strategy: DXB (+2/+3 on home) and GRU (−4/−5) are single-night stops, so I've anchored you to Madrid body time throughout and slept at "home night" hours. SIN (+7) is also never more than one full day, so the same applies — two split sleeps rather than a shift.
